$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F=(x+y)^{2}\,i+(y+z)^{2}\,j+(x+z)^{2}\,k.$ Evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((y+z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+z)^{2}) \\  & =2(x+y)+2(y+z)+2(x+z) \\  & =4(x+y+z).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,1,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(-2,1,-1) & =4((-2)+(1)+(-1)) \\  & =4\cdot (-2) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14129167/assets/4bf8de7e8719545b3d8abf5dc9fb4bc0c5f71034dba7186b7d9822d9e8be044d.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

I. $∇\cdot F=0$

II. $∇\cdot F>0$

III. $∇\cdot F<0$

IV. $F$ is solenoidal
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14129167/assets/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement III is true, whereas statements I and II are false. Notice that the lengths of the vector's $x$-components decrease as we move horizontally towards the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a sink at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Example: 
                    Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.$ 
Evaluate $\nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{3y}) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf {F}$ at the point $(1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+0}+3(1)^{2}{e}^{3(0)} \\  & =1+3 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,2,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf k$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((2x-y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((3y-2z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x-2z)^{2}) \\  & =4(2x-y)+6(3y-2z)-4(x-2z) \\  & =4x+14y-4z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf { F}$ at the point $(1,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(1,2,1) & =4(1)+14(2)-4(1) \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $\mathbf F?$

I. $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$

II. $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0$

III. $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F <                    0$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that $\textrm{div}\, \mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $\mathbf F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $\mathbf F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $\mathbf F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P\mathbin{:}$

- If $\mathbf F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $\nabla \cdot  \mathbf F > 0$ at $P.$

- If $\mathbf F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $\nabla \cdot  \mathbf F <         0$ at $P.$

- If $\mathbf F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $\nabla \cdot  \mathbf F =0$ at $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14129167/assets/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statements II and III are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $\mathbf F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement IV is true. Since $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 0$ everywhere, the vector field $\mathbf F$ is solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

If the first partial derivatives of $P$ and $Q$ exist, then the **divergence** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,$ is the scalar given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

Notice that if we define the differential operator $\nabla$ (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as 

$$
\nabla =  \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} +  \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y},
$$

 

then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by the dot product

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F.
$$

For example, suppose that the vector field $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\, \mathbf i + e^{yx} \, \mathbf j .
$$

Then, we can calculate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ using the dot product formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =∇\cdot F \\  & =(i\,\frac{∂}{∂x}+j\,\frac{∂}{∂y})\cdot (2xy\,i+{e}^{yx}\,j) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{yx}) \\  & =2y+x{e}^{yx}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Some Important Notes About the Divergence of a Vector Field
tutorials.problem:
There are a few things we should note about the divergence:

- We can only compute the divergence of a *vector* field, and a vector field's divergence is a *scalar* field. So if $G(x,y) = \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,$ then we have the following map:

$$
\underbrace{\,\,\,\mathbf F(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{vector field}} \mapsto\underbrace{\,\,\,G(x,y)\,\,\,}_{\textrm{scalar field}}
$$

In contrast, if $f(x,y)$ is a scalar field, then the statement $\textrm{div}\, f$ has no meaning.

- We can easily extend the notion of divergence to three dimensions. So, if $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j + R\,\mathbf k,$ then $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z},
$$

where the three-dimensional differential operator $\nabla$ is given by

$$
\nabla =  \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} +  \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}.
$$

- The divergence of a vector field at a point $P$ gives us helpful information about the tendency of the vector field to behave like a source or a sink at $P.$ We'll describe this in more detail shortly.

tutorials.name: Physical Interpretation of Divergence
tutorials.problem:
Our goal now is to develop an intuitive understanding of what the divergence of a vector field measures.

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ and the point $S,$ shown below. Imagine that this vector field represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14129167/assets/a785c84976242d699af11ab2203600e2007e95e35b60665ba9882c8f0f25bce3.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $S$ acts like a **source**. You can think of this as an open faucet, pushing water onto the plane and away from itself. 

Since $S$ acts like a source, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is nonzero. By convention, if a point $S$ acts like a source, the divergence is positive:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0
$$

In this particular case, *every* point in our vector field acts as a source. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F > 0$ everywhere.

If we reverse the situation, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14129167/assets/b4c923bbde36568e4e2f36f7d388622a520d0799d558049f72d0194e0bd679f7.png)

 

We can see from our diagram that $T$ acts like a **sink**. You can think of this as an open plughole that sucks in the surrounding water.

Since $T$ acts like a sink, $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F$ is also nonzero. By convention, if a point $T$ acts like a sink, the divergence is negative:

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0
$$

Every point in our vector field acts like a sink in this case. So $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F < 0$ everywhere.

Finally, note that if $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = 0$ everywhere in the domain of some vector field $\mathbf F,$ we say that $\mathbf F$ is **solenoidal.**

tutorials.name: Examples of Vector Field With Divergence and Solenoidal Vector Fields

Intuitively, the divergence of at a point measures how much acts like a source or a sink at

If everywhere in the domain of we say that is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

  • Statement I is true, whereas statements II and III are false. For any point the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, acts neither like a source nor a sink.

  • Statement IV is true. Since everywhere, the vector field is solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only."
